displayQuote: The mind is its own place, and in itself can make a heaven of hell, a hell of heaven

meta.title: Who really said "The mind is its own place, and in itself can make a heaven of hell, a hell of heaven"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — John Milton wrote it. It is Satan speaking in Paradise Lost, Book I (1667), lines 254–255. Verified against the primary text.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The mind is its own place, and in itself can make a heaven of hell, a hell of heaven'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Milton — but it's Satan's line in Paradise Lost, Book I (1667), lines 254–255, not the author's own counsel. Verified.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Milton. The line is spoken by Satan in Paradise Lost, Book I, lines 254–255 (first published 1667). The popular wording is a light spelling-modernization of Milton’s original, “The mind is its own place, and in it self / Can make a Heav’n of Hell, a Hell of Heav’n.”

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt:
Farewel happy Fields
Where Joy for ever dwells: Hail horrours, hail
Infernal world, and thou profoundest Hell
Receive thy new Possessor: One who brings
A mind not to be chang’d by Place or Time.
The mind is its own place, and in it self
Can make a Heav’n of Hell, a Hell of Heav’n.
trail: The line appears verbatim at Poets.org (Book I, lines 221–270), where the speaker is identified as the fallen archangel.
Wikisource’s 1674 text carries the identical lines at 254–255.
Wikiquote’s sourced Milton section cites it to “Paradise Lost, Book I, lines 254–255.”
source.excerptNote: Satan’s first speech on the burning lake. Nine lines later comes the poem’s other most-quoted boast: “Better to reign in Hell, then serve in Heav’n.”

source.rightsNote: Paradise Lost was first published in 1667 and revised in 1674; Milton died in 1674. The work has been in the public domain for centuries, so this original English wording is free to reproduce.

author.name: John Milton
author.heading: About John Milton
author.bio: John Milton (1608–1674) was an English poet and republican pamphleteer, best known for the blank-verse epic Paradise Lost (1667), which retells the Fall of Man. Blind for the last two decades of his life, he dictated the poem to amanuenses. His Satan — eloquent, defiant, self-deceiving — became one of the most debated characters in English literature, and lines like this one are among the most quoted in the language.

misattribution.heading: The catch
misattribution.intro: The words really are Milton’s — but they are almost always cited wrong in a subtler way: who is speaking, and why.

items.why: The line is a defiant boast by Satan, newly cast into Hell, talking himself into believing his fallen mind can reign anywhere. Quoted as stand-alone self-help — “stay positive, your mind makes your reality” — it inverts Milton’s intent, which is to dramatize how pride and self-deception rationalize damnation.
A widely circulated variant reads “a heaven of hell or a hell of heaven.” Milton wrote no “or” — the original balances the two clauses with a comma: “a Heav’n of Hell, a Hell of Heav’n.”

misattribution.truthLine: So: yes, John Milton wrote it — but it is Satan’s line in Paradise Lost, Book I, and the genuine text has no “or.”

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: Milton gives his Satan the finest rhetoric in the poem, and this couplet is the crown of it. Torn from the epic, it reads as a bracing lesson in mental resilience — the mind as sovereign over circumstance. In place, it is the sound of a proud spirit reasoning itself deeper into ruin.

That double life — inspirational surface, cautionary depth — is exactly why the line has been quoted for three and a half centuries, and why it is so often quoted against the grain of what Milton meant.
context.pull: “The mind is its own place” — a triumph of rhetoric spoken by the poem’s villain.
